title: Why everyone stands for a book

card.keepWhy: When the story opens, stand up.
sources: Nehemiah 8:1-12 (2 Esdras 8 in the Douay-Rheims): all the people gather as one man in the square before the Water Gate and ask Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses; he reads before the men and women and all who could understand, from early morning until midday; Ezra stands on a wooden pulpit made for the purpose, above all the people; when he opens the book, all the people stand up; Levites help the people understand, reading distinctly and giving the sense; the people weep on hearing the law; Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites say, “This day is holy to the Lord your God; do not mourn or weep … Go your way, eat the fat and drink sweet wine and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared … do not be grieved, for the joy of the Lord is your strength” (8:9-10, RSV); they go to celebrate “because they had understood the words” (8:12).
Ezra-Nehemiah setting: after the return from exile in Babylon.

General Instruction of the Roman Missal 60, 133-134 (the people stand for the Gospel; the three small signs of the cross on forehead, lips and breast); Sacrosanctum Concilium 7 (Christ is present in his word, since it is he himself who speaks when the scriptures are read in the Church).
Gospel: Old English godspel, “good news,” translating Greek euangelion. Homily: GIRM 65-66.
check: Ezra is painted only from behind or far away, as a precaution (some Muslim traditions honor Uzair). Confirm.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever stood up without being told to, like when a bride walks in, or a judge?
options: exactly. the body knows before the head does. listen.
that’s how most of us learn it. this story shows where it started.
keep watching. you’re about to see a whole city do it.

steps.line: After years in exile, the people came home to Jerusalem. They gathered in a city square and asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the book of God’s law.
Ezra climbed a wooden platform, high above the crowd, so everyone could see: men, women, anyone old enough to understand.

steps.q: Ezra opens the scroll, and the whole crowd rises to its feet. How long do you guess he reads to them?
steps.why: From first light to midday, Nehemiah says, and “the ears of all the people were attentive.” Hours on their feet, and nobody sat down.

steps.line: When he opened the book, all the people stood up. He read aloud from early morning until noon, and helpers explained it so everyone understood.
As they heard the words, the whole crowd began to weep.

steps.q: Thousands of people are in tears. What do Ezra and the leaders tell them?
o: Today is holy. Don’t cry, go and celebrate
Keep crying, because you broke these laws
Go home and fast until evening
steps.why: Not shame. A feast. Hearing the words was meant to bring joy.

steps.line: The leaders said, “This day is holy. Do not weep. Go, eat and drink, and send food to anyone who has none.” And the city celebrated.

steps.q: Ezra’s reading fell on the first day of the seventh month. What do Jews keep on that date today?
steps.why: The first of Tishrei. The leaders told the weeping crowd this day was for joy, “for the joy of the Lord is your strength.”

steps.line: Today, at Mass, people sit for the first readings. Then the whole room stands, often as the Gospel book is carried in, and the story of Jesus is read.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Catholics sit for the other readings but stand for the Gospel, the story of Jesus’s life. Why?
o: It’s the longest reading of the Mass
It was written by the apostles
Christ is believed to speak in it
steps.why: You stand when someone important walks in. Catholics believe that when the Gospel is read, Christ is the one speaking.

steps.q: The word Gospel comes from Old English. What did it first mean?
steps.why: Godspel: good + news, a translation of the Greek euangelion. “God’s story” is an old mix-up, and an easy one to make.

say: here’s what i love. the stand isn’t new. long before any church, a whole city rose the moment the book was opened.

catholics stand for the gospel because they believe Christ himself speaks when it’s read. right before, they trace three small crosses: forehead, lips, heart. one common way to say it: may these words be in my mind, on my lips, in my heart.

steps.q: Ezra’s helpers explained what was read, so everyone understood. What does that suggest about why a homily, a short talk, follows the Gospel at Mass?
o: The words are meant to be understood
It lets the priest add his own views
It splits the readings from the prayers
steps.why: Nehemiah says the helpers “gave the sense.” Read, then explain: from Ezra’s square to Sunday Mass, the words are meant to land.

today.say: next time you hear a story about jesus, at mass or right here, try the three small crosses first: forehead, lips, heart. you can watch others do it, learn it, or join in.
options: forehead, lips, heart. that’s how a whole room gets ready to listen.
I’ll watch for it at Mass
that counts. watching is how everyone learned it.
